prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit.

We represent: defendant.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that shotgun pleadings that fail to give defendants adequate notice of the claims against them should be dismissed.

Cite at least six decisions of the Eleventh Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. Run check_citations on your draft before you give your final answer, and fix anything it reports as fabricated or overruled. Use search_cases and get_case to look authorities up.
answer:
## ARGUMENT

### The Complaint Is a Shotgun Pleading That Fails to Give Defendant Adequate Notice and Should Be Dismissed.

Rule 8(a)(2) requires "a short and plain statement of the claim showing that the pleader is entitled to relief." Rule 10(b) requires a party to state its claims "in numbered paragraphs, each limited as far as practicable to a single set of circumstances." The Eleventh Circuit has long condemned complaints that disregard these rules. It calls them "shotgun pleadings." *See Weiland v. Palm Beach Cnty. Sheriff's Office*, 792 F.3d 1313, 1320–23 (11th Cir. 2015). The Eleventh Circuit has identified shotgun pleadings in its case law for decades. *See, e.g.*, *Anderson v. Dist. Bd. of Trs. of Cent. Fla. Cmty. Coll.*, 77 F.3d 364, 366–67 (11th Cir. 1996); *Cramer v. Florida*, 117 F.3d 1258, 1263 (11th Cir. 1997).

**A. The governing standard.** *Weiland* identified four rough categories of shotgun pleadings. The first is a complaint in which each count adopts the allegations of all preceding counts. The second is a complaint "replete with conclusory, vague, and immaterial facts not obviously connected to any particular cause of action." The third is a complaint that does not separate each cause of action into a different count. The fourth is a complaint that asserts multiple claims against multiple defendants without specifying which defendant is responsible for which acts. 792 F.3d at 1321–23; *accord Vibe Micro, Inc. v. Shabanets*, 878 F.3d 1291, 1294–95 (11th Cir. 2018). "The unifying characteristic of all types of shotgun pleadings is that they fail to one degree or another, and in one way or another, to give the defendants adequate notice of the claims against them and the grounds upon which each claim rests." *Weiland*, 792 F.3d at 1323. Notice is the touchstone. A complaint that leaves a defendant guessing which allegations support which claim does not satisfy Rules 8 and 10. *See Anderson*, 77 F.3d at 366–67.

**B. The Complaint falls within these categories.** [Plaintiff's] Complaint is a shotgun pleading in at least the following ways. *First*, each count "re-alleges and incorporates by reference" every preceding paragraph, including all prior counts. That makes the last count a combination of everything before it. *See Weiland*, 792 F.3d at 1321; *Anderson*, 77 F.3d at 366. *Second*, the Complaint combines several legal theories in single counts. *See Weiland*, 792 F.3d at 1322–23. *Third*, the Complaint lumps Defendant together with other defendants and attributes conduct to them collectively. It never says what Defendant itself did. *See id.* at 1323; *Magluta v. Samples*, 256 F.3d 1282, 1284 (11th Cir. 2001) (criticizing a complaint that was "replete with allegations that 'the defendants' engaged in certain conduct, making no distinction among the fourteen defendants charged"). Defendant cannot tell which factual allegations are meant to support the claims against it, so it cannot frame a meaningful response. [Insert record cites to specific paragraphs and counts.]

**C. Dismissal is the appropriate remedy.** Shotgun pleadings burden courts and opposing parties alike. They impede orderly discovery and consume judicial resources that other litigants need. *See Davis v. Coca-Cola Bottling Co. Consol.*, 516 F.3d 955, 979–81 (11th Cir. 2008); *Strategic Income Fund, L.L.C. v. Spear, Leeds & Kellogg Corp.*, 305 F.3d 1293, 1295 (11th Cir. 2002); *Vibe Micro*, 878 F.3d at 1295. For this reason, the Eleventh Circuit has instructed that a district court confronted with a shotgun pleading has the authority, and the duty, to require repleading. It should do so even when the defendant has not moved. *See Jackson v. Bank of Am., N.A.*, 898 F.3d 1348, 1357–58 (11th Cir. 2018); *Cramer*, 117 F.3d at 1263.

Defendant has no obligation to answer a pleading that violates Rules 8 and 10. The Court should dismiss the Complaint. Any leave to replead should be conditioned on the plaintiff curing each defect identified above. A cured pleading must (1) drop the blanket incorporation of earlier counts, (2) plead each cause of action in its own count, and (3) identify which defendant committed which acts. If the plaintiff fails to do so, the dismissal should be with prejudice. *See Vibe Micro*, 878 F.3d at 1295; *Weiland*, 792 F.3d at 1320–21.
